title: Quantum impurity models: easy at equilibrium, universal in motion
authors: Srinivasan Arunachalam, Sergey Bravyi, Anirban Chowdhury, Arkopal Dutt, Alexandru Gheorghiu, Zhi Li
abstract: A quantum impurity model describes a small interacting subsystem embedded into a large bath of free fermions. Here we study the computational complexity of calculating the ground energy, thermal equilibrium, and dynamical properties of these models. Our work reveals a sharp contrast: equilibrium properties can be efficiently approximated by classical means, whereas time evolution can implement a universal quantum computation. More precisely, let $H$ be the Hamiltonian of an impurity model with $n$ fermionic modes and a constant-size impurity. We show that: (1) the ground energy of $H$ can be approximated to additive error $\varepsilon$ by a classical algorithm with runtime $\textsf{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)$, improving on the quasi-polynomial runtime of the best previously known algorithm; (2) at inverse temperature $β$, the Helmholtz free energy and a classical description of the thermofield double state can be computed to precision $\varepsilon$ in time $\textsf{poly}(n,β,1/\varepsilon)$; (3) simulating the time evolution $e^{-iHt}$ is $\textsf{BQP}$-complete, for $H$ that is time-independent and has a fixed, constant impurity size. Our algorithms exploit exponential suppression of multi-particle bath excitations in a basis organized by energy scale and Krylov depth. Our universality construction realizes a stationary quantum processor whose program arrives in a stream of freely propagating fermions.
summary: This work analyzes quantum impurity models, showing that while calculating equilibrium properties like ground energy is classically tractable in polynomial time, simulating the system's time evolution is computationally hard (BQP-complete). The authors achieve this by developing specialized algorithms that exploit the structure of the fermionic bath excitations.
main_problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of calculating various properties (ground energy, thermal equilibrium, and dynamics) for quantum impurity models.
main_result: It establishes a sharp contrast: equilibrium properties can be efficiently approximated classically, while the time evolution simulation is proven to be BQP-complete.
method: The authors develop specialized algorithms exploiting the exponential suppression of multi-particle bath excitations using energy-scale and Krylov depth basis organization.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum impurity model, consisting of a small interacting subsystem (impurity) coupled to a large bath of free fermions, described by a Hamiltonian $H = H_0 + V$.
key_observables: Ground energy ($E_1(H)$), Helmholtz free energy ($F_ eta$), and the time evolution operator ($e^{-iHt}$).
important_parameters: Accuracy parameters ($\epsilon$, $\delta$), inverse temperature ($ eta$), and the size of the impurity ($m$, assumed constant).
main_assumptions: The impurity size $m$ is assumed to be fixed and constant for the strongest complexity results.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the complexity for ground energy (Theorem 1.1), thermal equilibrium (Theorems 1.2-1.4), and finally proves the BQP-completeness of the time evolution simulation (Theorem 1.5).
why_interesting: The demonstration that a physical quantum system's dynamics can realize a universal quantum processor is highly relevant for understanding quantum simulation capabilities and computational complexity boundaries.

After creating a small artificial gap ω > 0 in the bath Hamiltonian and changing the one-particle basis, the Hamiltonian is represented as a network of fermionic blocks indicated by boxes. Each box contains at most m fermionic modes, where m = O(1) is the impurity size. Each horizontal chain of boxes corresponds to a dyadic energy shell spanned by bath modes with excitation energies in [2pω, 2p+1ω) for some integer p ≥0.
